questions.stem: Which transport mechanism moves glucose from the tubular lumen to the epithelial cell?

evidence.quote: So, the sodium-glucose transporters, SGLT2 and SGLT1, um, those are located on the brush borders of the proximal tubule cells. Um, and again, they're, they're secondary active transporters.
Apical SGLT and NKCC2 are symporters.

questions.note:
**Glucose crosses the apical (luminal) membrane on SGLT2 and SGLT1, which are secondary active transporters riding the Na+ gradient made by the basolateral Na+/K+-ATPase.** The lecturer read this poll question and its five choices aloud at 00:22:52, then skipped it because the transporters hadn't been shown yet. The answer comes from slide 15 and the explanation about ten minutes later (00:32:55).

Primary active transport: false. That is the Na+/K+-ATPase itself, which spends ATP directly. It builds the gradient but doesn't carry glucose.

Secondary active transport: true. SGLTs on the brush border move glucose uphill using energy stored in the Na+ gradient.

Facilitated diffusion: false. That is how glucose leaves the cell across the basolateral membrane, through GLUT2 and GLUT1.

Simple diffusion: false. Glucose needs a carrier protein to cross either membrane.

Osmosis: false. Osmosis is water movement, not glucose.

questions.stem: If you were to see a question about anything having to do with glucose, changing the amount of glucose that either gets reabsorbed or secreted, which one do you think is going to have a bigger effect, inhibiting SGLT2 or SGLT-1?

evidence.quote: SGLT 2. OK. So if you ever see a question where some are saying like buy SGLT2, some buy SGLT1, um, you can easily eliminate SGLT1.
Um, 90% of the glucose is reabsorbed using the SGLT2, which is in the very early part of the proximal convoluted tubule.
No useful drug that inhibits SGLT-1 because it doesn't do much.
Apical SGLT2 in the early proximal tubule reabsorbs most filtered glucose.

questions.note:
**SGLT2 does about 90% of glucose reabsorption in the early proximal tubule (S1), so blocking it matters far more.** The lecturer asked this aloud with the two options built into the question and gave the answer right after. Turned into a two-choice item from that passage.

Inhibiting SGLT2: true. It carries most of the filtered glucose, which is why SGLT2 inhibitors cause glucosuria.

Inhibiting SGLT1: false. SGLT1 in the late proximal tubule (S3) only picks up the remaining ~10%. The lecturer's tip: on a question, an SGLT1 answer can almost always be eliminated.
